item.title: Comparative Analysis of Influencing Factors for Diverse Urban Renewal: Evidence From Beijing's Built‐Up Areas
item.description:
Tingyue Deng, Fengping An, Jing Zhang, Shan Xu
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70405
ABSTRACT Investigating the influencing factors of urban renewal and their differences across renewal types helps optimize resource allocation. Existing studies have analyzed the influencing factors of multiple types of urban renewal, but have not yet identified the differences in the effects of these factors across different renewal types or tested the statistical significance of such differences. Therefore, this study selects multiple influencing factors from three dimensions—location environment, social services, and economic foundation—and constructs a multinomial logistic regression model to analyze the effects of these factors on four types of urban renewal: commercial and office renewal, public service facility renewal, park and green space renewal, and residential renewal. Meanwhile, Wald tests are used to examine the statistical significance of the differences in the effects of each influencing factor across different renewal types. The results show that: (1) land price is an important influencing factor for all types of urban renewal, while factors such as the distance from renewal points to major roads and the density of transportation facilities exhibit differentiated effects; (2) in the comparison of statistically significant differences in influencing effects, the relationships among different renewal types mainly present three patterns: “single comparison,” “single radiation,” and “multiple intersection”; and (3) a comprehensive comparison of the influencing factors of different urban renewal types and their differences indicates that urban renewal is jointly guided by the dual cores of government and market forces, driven by both ecological and social demands, and promoted through interactions among multiple stakeholders.

item.title: Unsupervised Patch‐Based Ecoregion Classification in Austria Using DEM ‐Derived Features, Deep Learning, and Climate Data
item.description:
Thomas Schneidergruber, Johannes Scholz
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70421
ABSTRACT Digital elevation models (DEMs) are widely used to characterize terrain and support applications ranging from geomorphology to environmental management. While traditional analyses rely on handcrafted geomorphometric features, advances in machine learning enable richer, data‐driven representations of topographic surfaces. In this study, we present a multi‐source feature fusion approach that integrates statistical descriptors of elevation, derived terrain attributes, deep features extracted via a ResNet encoder, and climate variables from weather datasets. Using 5175 randomly sampled patches, we generated a comprehensive feature set and applied unsupervised clustering to identify ecoregional units. Results indicate that combining DEM‐derived features with climate data produces clusters that are both quantitatively robust, as indicated by internal validity indices, and exhibit meaningful spatial distribution when compared with known ecoregions.

item.title: Cartographic Storytelling for the “2Ws and 1H” in Flood Perception: An Interactive and Time‐Varying Evacuation Plan for the General Public
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Disaster maps play an essential role in disseminating risk information to the general public. However, conventional disaster maps usually present static flood information, making it difficult to translate flood risk information into individualized and actionable evacuation decisions. This article adopts the idea of cartographic storytelling and proposes a time‐varying coupling approach that links flood simulation outputs with dynamic evacuation route planning for residents. Specifically, the proposed approach updates building risk states as the flood evolves and simultaneously plans routes to shelters according to current conditions and potential risks, thereby transforming complex spatiotemporal flood dynamics into tailored evacuation route recommendations that answer the “2Ws and 1H” questions of public evacuation, namely when to evacuate, where to go, and how to reach a shelter. Finally, a section of the Rhine River in Bonn, Germany, is selected for experimental analysis. The experimental results show that the proposed approach not only presents flood information but also provides actionable insights throughout the evolution of the flood, supporting the public to understand dynamic flood risk changes and take clearer and more timely evacuation actions during flood events. Our findings could support the development of interactive evacuation tools for residents during floods, as well as rescue management and disaster education.

ABSTRACT

Disaster maps play an essential role in disseminating risk information to the general public. However, conventional disaster maps usually present static flood information, making it difficult to translate flood risk information into individualized and actionable evacuation decisions. Specifically, the proposed approach updates building risk states as the flood evolves and simultaneously plans routes to shelters according to current conditions and potential risks, thereby transforming complex spatiotemporal flood dynamics into tailored evacuation route recommendations that answer the “2Ws and 1H” questions of public evacuation, namely when to evacuate, where to go, and how to reach a shelter. The experimental results show that the proposed approach not only presents flood information but also provides actionable insights throughout the evolution of the flood, supporting the public to understand dynamic flood risk changes and take clearer and more timely evacuation actions during flood events. Our findings could support the development of interactive evacuation tools for residents during floods, as well as rescue management and disaster education.
